title: Spanish Pensioner Evicted Abroad Set to Return Home, Lawyer Announces — DW.com
body:
The 87‑year‑old Madrid resident Maricarmen García Álvarez, whose forced removal from a long‑time home ignited a wave of protests across Spain, will be allowed to move back into her apartment, her lawyer announced on Thursday. The decision, reached after a week‑long legal battle, marks a rare victory for a senior citizen caught in the country’s escalating housing crisis and could set a precedent for other vulnerable tenants facing eviction.

Maricarmen’s eviction on 21 May shocked the nation. The woman, who had lived in the same third‑floor flat in the historic Lavapiés district for more than four decades, was served a court order to vacate after the building’s owner claimed unpaid rent and sought to sell the property. The case quickly became a rallying point for housing activists, trade unions and ordinary citizens, who staged sit‑ins, marched through the capital and flooded social media with the hashtag #NoAlDesalojo. Demonstrators argued that the eviction highlighted a systemic problem: rising rents, speculative property sales and a legal framework that often favours landlords over elderly or low‑income tenants.

Legal experts say Maricarmen’s successful appeal hinges on a combination of procedural errors and newly introduced tenant‑protection measures. Her attorney, Ana López, pointed out that the original eviction notice failed to comply with the mandatory “pre‑eviction mediation” requirement introduced in 2022, which obliges landlords to attempt an out‑of‑court settlement before proceeding to court. Moreover, the judge noted that the landlord’s claim of arrears was based on a disputed accounting of utility charges, further weakening the case. “The court recognized that an 87‑year‑old with limited means cannot be expected to navigate complex billing disputes on her own,” López said.

The broader context of Spain’s housing market underscores why Maricarmen’s story resonated so strongly. Over the past decade, Spain has seen a 30 percent increase in average rent prices in major cities, while the supply of affordable housing has lagged behind demand. The pandemic amplified these trends, as many landlords sought to recoup lost income by raising rents or selling properties to investors. In response, the government introduced a series of reforms, including rent caps in certain municipalities and stronger tenant rights, but critics argue that enforcement remains uneven and that many seniors continue to be displaced.

Activist groups have welcomed the ruling as a morale boost but caution against complacency. “This is a win for Maricarmen, but it does not solve the systemic imbalance that leaves thousands of older Spaniards at risk of losing their homes each year,” said Carlos Méndez, spokesperson for the housing coalition Alianza por la Vivienda. He urged lawmakers to accelerate the implementation of a national “right to housing” law, which would guarantee a minimum period of tenancy security and provide state‑funded legal assistance for elderly tenants.

Looking ahead, Maricarmen’s return to her flat is expected to occur within the next few days, pending a formal handover from the building’s management. Her case may inspire other tenants to challenge evictions, especially as courts become more vigilant about procedural compliance. At the same time, the episode adds pressure on Spain’s parliament to finalize pending housing legislation before the end of the year. If the momentum generated by Maricarmen’s ordeal translates into concrete policy changes, it could reshape the balance of power between landlords and tenants and offer a more humane safety net for the nation’s aging population.
